title.official: Who may request review of lawyer’s charges

division.heading: Lawyers’ Charges, Retainer Agreements and Right of Review

operative_text.controlling:
10.11   A lawyer’s charges may be reviewed in Alberta
(a) at the request of a client if
(i) the lawyer resides in Alberta,
(ii) the lawyer’s principal office is in Alberta,
(iii) the lawyer’s charges specify an Alberta address for
the lawyer or the law firm of the lawyer,
(iv) most of the services were performed in Alberta,
(v) the services were performed in connection with legal
proceedings commenced in Alberta in which the
lawyer was a lawyer of record, or
(vi) the retainer agreement between the lawyer and the
client so provides,
and
(b) at the request of the lawyer if
(i) the client resides in Alberta,
(ii) the principal office or place of business of the client
is in Alberta,
(iii) most of the services were performed in Alberta and
the lawyer has no office in the jurisdiction outside
Alberta where the client resides or carries on
business, or
(iv) the retainer agreement between the lawyer and the
client so provides.

BOOK_A.title: Who May Request Review of Lawyer’s Charges
BOOK_A.commentary:
A lawyer can have the court review his or her own bill either to get execution (enforcement), or
to demonstrate that it is appropriate.²
A client is presumed liable to pay his or her lawyer (counsel or solicitor), even if someone else
(such as an insurer) has also agreed to do so. But the lay client is not the only one liable to pay.
A lawyer who retained another lawyer (as distant agent or as counsel) is also presumed liable to
pay.³
And often other persons contract to pay solicitor-client costs, e. g. mortgagors, or those who
agree to pay costs as part of a settlement. The expanded deﬁnition of “client” in the Appendix lets
them have the account reviewed in the same way that the client could, though thorny issues of
privilege may then arise.⁴
A bill to an executor by counsel hired by him was approved by the executor. A mere beneﬁciary
of the estate was unable to have the legal bill reviewed. Her right was to have the executor’s
accounts and fee taxed, not the counsel’s bill?⁵

Because the injured plaintiff and his solicitor have a proprietary interest in the material which
they have generated and it costs money, the Minister of Hospitals with a subrogated claim should
reimburse them for a proportionate share of the out-of-pocket expenses paid to third parties and
incurred in obtaining material such as experts’ reports.¹
Review is a remedial order, and so it interrupts or restarts the limitation period for a lawyer to
sue his client for fees.²
Does the liberality of the review of fees depend on whether a non-client or a trust is to pay
them?³
The mere fact that there is usually privilege involved in communications between a lawyer and
his or her client does not bar the lawyer from having the account reviewed if the client does not
pay it. Nor does it bar such a review at the instance of the successor in title of the lawyer, such as
a legally appointed Custodian of his practice.⁴
In addition, reviews are usually held in the private
meeting room or ofﬁce of the reviewing ofﬁcer, and though the reviewing ofﬁcer may borrow the
ﬁle or papers of the lawyer, invariably the ofﬁcer returns them at the end, and never puts them on
the public court ﬁle.⁵
If a solicitor is an estate trustee and takes fees from it without prior court approval, a successor
trustee can have the court later review the fees and order part refunded.⁶

BOOK_C.title: Who may request review of lawyer’s charges

commentary.text:
The review process is available as between lawyers and clients. It allows fee matters to be reviewed in a different, and in some ways less public, forum than in a civil action. Borden Ladner Gervais LLP v. CBI Investments Ltd., [2015] A.J. No. 782, 2015 ABQB 442 at para. 8 (Alta. Q.B.), affd [2016] A.J. No. 388, 2016 ABQB 220 (Alta. Q.B.).
The term “client” as used in this rule could mean any person to whom a lawyer has rendered an account for lawyer’s charges, and a person who is or may be liable to pay or who has paid lawyer’s charges or part of them. Fleming v. Fleming Alberta , [2020] A.J. No. 142, 2020 ABQB 85 at para. 26 (Alta. Q.B.); Treasury Branches v. 1401057 Alberta Ltd (c.o.b. Katch 22) . , [2013] A.J. No. 1449, 2013 ABQB 748 at footnote 3 (Alta. Q.B.); and definitions (contained in an appendix to those rules). Alberta Rules of Court The assessment process is effectively a modified trial process. Parties are heard, evidence is tendered, and a decision is made by an unbiased party. The assessment process is a release valve that serves both the legal profession and the community. Matters that would otherwise burden an over-worked judicial system are funnelled directly to an expert adjudicator, doing away with the need for a protracted trial process at the superior courts. Further, it often prevents lawyers from being reported to the Law Society. It is a tool with tangible benefits for
